result: Acquired amputees maintain typical missing hand representation in SI despite varying phantom sensations. Mean dissimilarity in amputees was slightly reduced compared to controls (t(28)=1.13, p=0.27, BF=0.772) but significantly greater than congenital one-handers (t(29)=3.54, p=0.001). Typicality in amputees (rho=0.75) was not significantly different from controls (t(28)=0.991, p=0.33, BF=0.128), indicating preserved organization after an average of 18 years of handlessness.
evaluation: Claims C2, C21-C26, C70-C71 provide converging statistical evidence from RSA analysis showing preserved hand representation in amputees. The Bayesian analysis (BF=0.128) provides additional support for the null hypothesis of no difference from controls. The statistical tests are appropriate, sample sizes are adequate (n=18 amputees, n=12 controls), and multiple measures (dissimilarity and typicality) converge on the same conclusion.

result: Congenital one-handers show significantly reduced missing hand representation compared to both amputees and controls. Congenital one-handers showed no differentiation between digits (mean dissimilarity not different from 0; t(12)=0.73, p=0.48), significantly reduced dissimilarity versus controls (t(23)=4.86, p<0.001), and diminished typicality (mean rho=0.29) compared to both controls (t(23)=5.86, p<0.001) and amputees (t(29)=6.09, p<0.001).
evaluation: Claims C3, C23-C24, C27-C28, C100 provide consistent statistical evidence across multiple measures showing absent or severely reduced hand representation in congenital one-handers. The statistical tests are appropriate with adequate sample size (n=13), and the pattern is consistent across dissimilarity and typicality measures. This provides strong evidence for the role of early sensory experience.

result: Phantom kinaesthesia (motor control over phantom hand) positively correlates with typicality of missing hand representation in amputees. Stepwise regression identified kinaesthesia as the only significant predictor (β=0.07, t=4.46, p<0.001, adjusted R²=0.645), confirmed by bootstrapping (96.3% inclusion rate). Post-hoc correlation was significant (rho=0.72, p=0.001), while no correlation was found with phantom vividness (rho=0.13, p=0.61) or years since amputation (rho=0.17, p=0.49).
evaluation: Claims C4, C38-C45, C102 provide robust statistical evidence from multiple analyses (stepwise regression, bootstrapping, correlation, partial correlation) all converging on the relationship between kinaesthesia and typicality. The bootstrapping validation (96.3%) strengthens confidence in the regression model. The specificity of the relationship (no correlation with other phantom measures) supports the interpretation.

result: Missing hand representation persists in amputees even after phantom sensations have diminished. Three amputees with weak/no chronic phantom vividness (<10/100) showed high typicality (average rho=0.83), significantly stronger than congenital one-handers (Mann-Whitney U=38, p=0.007) and not different from controls (Mann-Whitney U=29, p=0.52, BF=0.089). The regression intercept (β=0.52) predicts retained representation even at zero kinaesthesia.
evaluation: Claims C47-C51, C72 provide evidence from subset analysis and regression modeling. While the subset is small (n=3), the effect sizes are large and consistent with the regression prediction. The Bayesian analysis supports equivalence with controls. However, the small sample size for the subset analysis is a limitation, though the convergence with regression predictions strengthens the conclusion.

result: Ipsilateral intact hand representation in the missing hand cortex is preserved in amputees but reduced in congenital one-handers. Amputees showed no significant difference from controls in ipsilateral dissimilarity (t(28)=1.42, p=0.166, BF=0.209) or typicality (t(28)=0.69, p=0.498, BF=0.244). Congenital one-handers showed significantly lower ipsilateral representation than amputees for both dissimilarity (t(29)=3.81, p<0.001) and typicality (t(29)=3.05, p=0.005).
evaluation: Claims C61-C64, C95 provide consistent statistical evidence using an alternative task that controls for task demands across groups. The Bayesian analyses support equivalence between amputees and controls. The significant differences for congenital one-handers provide converging evidence for reduced missing hand representation using an indirect measure, strengthening the main findings.

result: Digit dissimilarity in congenital one-handers' missing hand area likely reflects task demands rather than sensorimotor representation. While cross-validated dissimilarity was significantly greater than zero (t(12)=2.51, p=0.027), congenital one-handers showed no significant differences between SI and visual area V5 for dissimilarity (t(12)=-1.03, p=0.322) or typicality (t(12)=0.78, p=0.448), whereas amputees and controls showed significant SI vs. V5 differences (all p's<0.02), resulting in a significant group×area interaction (dissimilarity: F(2,85)=4.25, p=0.018; typicality: F(2,85)=4.42, p=0.015).
evaluation: Claims C65-C69 provide important control analysis using V5 as a non-sensorimotor region. The lack of difference between SI and V5 in congenital one-handers, contrasted with significant differences in the other groups, supports the interpretation that residual dissimilarity in congenital one-handers reflects non-specific task effects. The group×area interaction provides statistical support for this interpretation.

result: Once cortical organization is formed through early sensory experience, it is remarkably persistent despite long-term attenuation of peripheral signals. The authors conclude that early-life experience is potentially necessary to create typical functional sensory organization, but not to maintain it, and suggest this may be a common organizing principle across sensory systems.
evaluation: Claims C5, C74, C99, C101, C103 represent the main conclusions drawn from the experimental findings. These conclusions are well-supported by the convergence of evidence from multiple analyses comparing acquired amputees (who had early experience) with congenital one-handers (who lacked early experience). The inference is logical and consistent with the data, though the generalization to other sensory systems (C101) relies on cited literature rather than direct evidence from this study.

result: M1 shows similar patterns to SI but with weaker digit individuation. Congenital one-handers showed significantly lower dissimilarity (t(23)=4.23, p<0.001) and typicality (t(23)=3.42, p=0.002; t(29)=3.50, p=0.002) compared to controls and amputees respectively. Amputees showed no significant differences from controls in dissimilarity (t(28)=0.53, p=0.60, BF=0.325) or typicality (t(28)=0.11, p=0.91, BF=0.253).
evaluation: Claims C29-C35 provide consistent evidence that M1 shows similar group differences as SI, though with weaker effects as expected from prior literature. The statistical tests are appropriate and the Bayesian analyses support equivalence between amputees and controls. This provides converging evidence across multiple cortical regions.

result: Split-half reliability analysis shows significantly lower consistency in congenital one-handers (rho=-0.02) compared to amputees (rho=0.41, p=0.001) and controls (rho=0.52, p=0.001), indicating no strongly consistent digit information in the missing hand area during this task.
evaluation: Claims C36-C37 provide additional evidence for lack of consistent digit representation in congenital one-handers using split-half reliability. The statistical tests are appropriate and the interpretation is conservative, acknowledging the reduced power from data splitting. This provides methodological validation of the main findings.

result: All participants, including congenital one-handers, showed some engagement of the missing/nondominant hand area. Congenital one-handers showed reduced SI activity compared to controls (t(23)=3.5, p=0.002) but activity was significantly greater than baseline (t(12)=2.6, p=0.02).
evaluation: Claims C18-C20 provide univariate activity analysis showing that all groups could engage the hand area, though congenital one-handers showed reduced activity. The statistical tests are appropriate and this provides important context that the lack of digit differentiation in congenital one-handers is not simply due to inability to activate the region.

result: All three groups performed the intact hand digit movement task equally well (congenital one-handers: 81.1%, amputees: 74.2%, controls: 75.3%; all comparisons p>0.26) and showed high representational typicality for the intact hand in SI (controls: rho=0.85, amputees: rho=0.81, congenital one-handers: rho=0.89; all comparisons p>0.11).
evaluation: Claims C57-C58, C111-C113 provide important control analyses showing equivalent task performance and intact hand representation across groups. This rules out general motor or cognitive deficits as explanations for group differences in missing hand representation. The statistical tests are appropriate and sample sizes adequate.

result: The study tested 18 acquired amputees (mean 18 years since amputation, mean chronic phantom vividness 58±38/100), 13 congenital one-handers (no phantom sensations), and 12 two-handed controls. Phantom sensation measures showed excellent inter-study consistency (ICC=0.79, 95% CI: 0.48-0.93, p<0.001) for 14 amputees who participated in prior studies.
evaluation: Claims C104-C110 provide demographic and methodological details. The sample sizes are adequate for the statistical tests performed. The reliability analysis (C110) is important for validating the phantom sensation measures. The groups are reasonably well-matched for age, though gender and handedness distributions vary somewhat.

result: MRI data was acquired at 3T using multiband imaging with high spatial (2mm isotropic) and temporal (TR=1500ms) resolution covering the whole brain. ROIs were not significantly different in size across groups (SI: F=1.27, p=0.29; M1: F=1.37, p=0.27).
evaluation: Claims C114-C117 provide methodological details about MRI acquisition and ROI definition. The acquisition parameters are appropriate for the study aims. The verification that ROI sizes did not differ across groups is an important control. These are standard methodological details that are adequately documented.

result: Prior work established that amputees with vivid phantom sensations maintain cortical hand representation and that structured peripheral input is not required for preserving sensorimotor hand representation. Phantom limb movements elicit distinct motor signals and three amputees with exceptionally vivid phantoms maintained digit order and extent of missing hand maps in SI at 7T.
evaluation: Claims C1, C14-C17 summarize prior work from the authors and others, supported by appropriate citations. These provide important context and motivation for the current study. The citations appear accurate and the characterization of prior findings is consistent with the cited literature.

result: Background on somatotopic organization: Adjacent body parts are represented proximally on the cortical sheet, neighboring digits are represented closer together, and representational structure reflects natural statistics of hand use. Concurrent inputs increase similarity while individuation increases dissimilarity, and alterations can affect perception and action.
evaluation: Claims C6-C13 provide background on somatotopic organization and representational structure, all supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These are well-established principles in the field and the citations are appropriate. This provides necessary theoretical context for interpreting the results.

result: Theoretical framework for ipsilateral representation: In controls, ipsilateral finger movements produce individuated digit representation that overlaps with contralateral hand representation and disappears during asymmetric bimanual movements, suggesting ipsilateral representation recruits contralateral hand representation. This predicts amputees should show similar ipsilateral representation as controls if missing hand representation persists, while congenital one-handers should show reduced ipsilateral representation.
evaluation: Claims C53-C56, C59-C60 provide theoretical framework based on cited literature (Diedrichsen et al.) and derive testable predictions. The logic is sound and the predictions follow from the theoretical framework. The citations are appropriate and the framework provides strong justification for using ipsilateral representation as an indirect measure of missing hand representation.

result: Discussion of mechanisms: Restored peripheral input can reinstate hand representation, suggesting canonical representation is immutable. The SI hand map can persist independently of peripheral input. The SI representation pattern is likely driven by motor efferent inputs and corollary discharge, which would not form in congenital one-handers who never operated a hand.
evaluation: Claims C75-C82 provide mechanistic interpretation of the findings, supported by citations and logical inference from the data. The proposed mechanism involving motor efference and corollary discharge is plausible and consistent with cited literature. However, this remains somewhat speculative as the study did not directly test these mechanisms.

result: Discussion of reorganization: Sensory deprivation causes cortical reorganization in development and adulthood. Original reports emphasized facial remapping as maladaptive, later challenged in favor of intact hand representation as adaptive. The authors propose reorganization does not necessarily abolish original functional layout, with persistent representation and reorganization potentially engaging separate cortical layers, though their interaction remains to be determined.
evaluation: Claims C83-C93 provide extensive discussion of reorganization literature and propose a framework for reconciling persistent representation with reorganization. The historical review is accurate based on citations. The proposal (C91-C92) is speculative but plausible and acknowledges uncertainty (C93). This provides important theoretical context though it goes beyond the direct evidence of the study.

result: Discussion of ipsilateral intact hand representation: The missing hand cortex in amputees responds to intact hand inputs. However, ipsilateral dissimilarity was not significantly greater in amputees than controls, inconsistent with adaptive reorganization interpretation. While phantom hand maps activate independently of the intact hand, structured inputs from the intact hand via ipsilateral pathways might sustain the missing hand map.
evaluation: Claims C94, C96-C98 discuss ipsilateral representation findings and their interpretation. C96 notes inconsistency with prior adaptive reorganization interpretation, which is a valid observation. However, C98 is speculative about ipsilateral inputs sustaining the missing hand map, and this mechanism was not directly tested. The interpretation requires additional evidence to be conclusive.

result: It is possible that congenital one-handers have typical sensorimotor representation of their missing hand but did not access it due to unnatural task demands, analogous to findings in congenitally blind individuals regarding visual cortex organization.
evaluation: Claim C52 raises an important alternative explanation that the task may not have been appropriate for congenital one-handers. While the ipsilateral hand task (C59-C60) was designed to address this concern and showed consistent results, this alternative explanation cannot be completely ruled out. The analogy to visual cortex in blind individuals is interesting but the situations may not be directly comparable.

result: The persistent hand representation observed in amputees does not reflect mere cognitive task demands such as visual feedback or attention, as evidenced by the contrast with congenital one-handers who performed the same task.
evaluation: Claim C73 makes an important inference that the group differences rule out cognitive task demands as the sole explanation. This is supported by the comparison with congenital one-handers who performed the same task with similar behavioral performance (C57, C111-C112) but showed different neural patterns. The citations to Kuehn et al. and Puckett et al. provide additional context.
